title: Bhishma's vow

segments.voice: Yesterday in Bhishma's vow: one word, mother, a chariot ride to Hastinapura, and the kings saying, he is truly Bhishma. Who did you tell what they mean to you? Day seven hundred fifteen.

Shantanu has just heard everything his son did at the fisherman's house: the throne given away, the lifelong vow, the bride brought home and called mother. Bhishma asked for nothing in return. He only told his father what he had done. Now his father gives him something anyway, and it's rare: a say over his own death. Death will not come to you, the king tells him, in the text's sense, as long as you wish to live.
screen: `A GIFT FROM FATHER TO SON.` → `HE ASKED FOR NOTHING.` → `DEATH ONLY WITH HIS LEAVE.`

segments.voice: The text says Shantanu was pleased by the hard thing his son had done. And he gives him a boon: death will never approach you while you want to live. It will come only when you give it leave. Tradition calls this icchamrityu, death at will. Look at the shape of the exchange. The son gave away his future: a crown, a marriage, children of his own. The father answers with power over the one thing no one usually gets to choose: the end of his own life. A man who has given up the next generation is given the right to decide how long his own will run. And reach back once more. When Vasishtha softened his curse, he said the Vasu who took the cow would live long on earth. Now the long life is in Bhishma's own hands. That's the last piece of Bhishma's vow, and it's a good place to let the story breathe, because readers have taken this vow more than one way. In some retellings and in some homes, Bhishma's vow is held up as devotion to a father, a son putting his parent's happiness above his own. Some readers have asked harder questions: about a king who let his son pay that price for his own wish, and about how much one promise should bind a life. The Mahabharata doesn't settle it here. It gives us the vow, the flowers, the name, the word mother, and the boon, and then it moves on to the bride herself. Her story begins long before this marriage.
screen: `THE KING IS PLEASED.` · `DEATH ONLY WHEN HE ALLOWS IT.` · `HE GAVE AWAY HIS FUTURE.` · `READ MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · then, large: `THE LONG LIFE IN HIS OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: Let the body be still, and simply watch the breath. Notice where each breath begins, and where it ends. You don't decide its length. It arrives, it rests, it goes. Follow one breath all the way in and all the way out, then another. If your mind runs ahead, come back to the edge of the breath you're on. Stay with beginnings and endings, gently, for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma's vow. A son's promise to his father, answered with a father's boon: death will come to him only with his leave.
Your line: Bhishma's vow. Today, thank someone out loud for something they gave up for you. Day seven hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Some Hindus remember Bhishma on a day called Bhishma Ashtami, offering water in his name, a rite usually made for one's own ancestors, since he left no children to make it for him.

fork.setup: you're Shantanu. your son gave up the throne and any children of his own so you could marry. what do you do?
options: accept, and give him a boon.
fork.reveal: pleased by the hard thing he did, Shantanu grants him death at will: it will come only with Bhishma's leave.

original.note: Sanskrit icchāmṛtyu, death at will: the name tradition gives Shantanu's boon to Bhishma.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bhishma's vow is only about what he gave up.
what it means: it ends with a father's gift: death will come only when Bhishma allows it.
what a scholar hears: Vasishtha's word of a long life on earth comes back as Shantanu's boon, which tradition calls icchamrityu.
